# Technical report: will a small fire keep burning in habitat air?

*Ember, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Every number below is regenerated by the commands in the last section.*

## Problem

Moon and Mars habitats are planned with more oxygen at lower pressure than the ISS (for example 34 % O₂ at 8.2 psi,
against 21 % at 14.7 psi). In microgravity there is no buoyant flow, so flammability data from Earth is a poor guide.
We ask whether a small fire keeps burning under such conditions, using only NASA's own experiments, and where the
evidence ends. Hypotheses: **H1** more oxygen raises the chance a flame keeps burning; **H2** oxygen percentage
predicts the outcome better than oxygen partial pressure; **H3** a model of the test conditions predicts unseen test
campaigns better than a constant baseline.

## Data

19 experimental tables from NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), each pinned by a SHA-256 checksum: 1,903 rows
read, 55 excluded (44 duplicate test identifiers, 11 impossible values), **1,848 kept**; rows that look odd keep a written
warning flag (flags by rule: 131 missing outcome, 7 implausible, 6 gas fractions not summing to 100 %, 1 extinction
diameter larger than the start). Cleaning rule: *flag, never silently fix*; checks run before unit conversion; nothing is imputed.

Only two tables record both the conditions and whether the flame survived:

| Table | What it models | Tests with an outcome | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| CFI-G, PSI-159 (gas-jet flames) | a small gas leak that ignites | 133 (31 stayed lit), 11 campaigns | 18–40 % O₂, 7.3–44 psi |
| FLEX, PSI-69 (fuel droplets) | a spilled liquid that ignites | 206 (27 burned to the end), 12 campaigns | 12–34 % O₂, 10–45 psi, up to 70 % CO₂ or 45 % helium |

The other 17 tables (solids, smoke, daily summaries) serve as evidence and coverage only. One non-NASA source, ZARM
drop-tower flame-spread data (doi:10.5281/zenodo.18479713), is kept apart and trains nothing.

## Method

- **Inputs.** Gas jets: oxygen %, pressure, fuel flow, carbon atoms in the fuel (2–4) and the fuel's share of the jet
  (0.3, 0.5, 1). Droplets: oxygen %, pressure, initial diameter, fuel, CO₂ % and helium %. Standardised within each
  training fold; no class rebalancing (it distorts probabilities); no imputation.
- **Models.** Logistic regression, a random forest (400 trees, minimum leaf 3) and a Gaussian process classifier with
  one length scale per input, against a constant baseline (23 % for gas jets, 13 % for droplets).
- **Selection rule, fixed in advance.** Usable only if it beats the baseline on both Brier score and log loss on
  unseen campaigns; the usable model with the lowest log loss is chosen.
- **Validation.** Grouped 5-fold cross-validation with the NASA test campaign as the group, repeated over 10
  partitions. Random splits would overstate skill, because near-repeat tests from one campaign would sit on both sides.
- **Uncertainty.** The chosen model is refitted on 15 campaign-bootstrap samples; the 10th–90th percentile is the range.
  Regression intervals (90 %) come from the errors on unseen campaigns.
- **Applicability domain** (OECD QSAR principle 3). Each request is placed by its standardised distance to tests of the
  same fuel: *tested* within the median nearest-neighbour distance, *estimated* inside every tested range and within
  twice the 95th percentile of the mean 5-nearest-neighbour distance, otherwise *untested* (also at any gravity other
  than microgravity), where no number is given.
- **Model-free checks.** Fisher's exact test, leave-one-campaign-out stability, and a count of tests in the 25–33 % O₂ band.

## Results

| Model (10 partitions) | Gas jets AUC | Gas Brier | Droplets AUC | Droplet Brier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 0.500 | 0.179 | 0.500 | 0.114 |
| Logistic regression | 0.815 ± 0.023 | 0.132 | 0.757 ± 0.029 | 0.115 (does not beat baseline) |
| Random forest | 0.809 ± 0.031 | 0.130 | 0.760 ± 0.016 | 0.101 |
| **Gaussian process (chosen)** | **0.830 ± 0.032** | **0.123** | **0.838 ± 0.013** | **0.094** |

- **H1, threshold and gap.** No gas flame stayed lit below 30 % O₂: 0 of 41, against 29 of 89 at 35–40 % (Fisher exact
  p = 5.4 × 10⁻⁶). Lowest O₂ at which one stayed lit: 33.2 %, stable at 33.2–35.4 % with any campaign left out. There
  are **no** gas-jet tests with an outcome between 25 % and 33 % O₂, the Moon-base range.
- **H2.** Oxygen percentage predicts far better than partial pressure (gas AUC 0.815 vs 0.649; droplets 0.757 vs 0.692),
  consistent with NASA materials testing (Harper et al., NTRS 20160004937).
- **H3.** All three models beat the baseline on gas jets (within about 0.02 AUC of each other, the size of the spread);
  on droplets the Gaussian process leads by about 0.08 AUC. Calibration slopes 1.00 (gas) and 0.90 (droplets).
- **Regressions** beat their baselines: droplet burning-rate constant MAE 0.059 vs 0.112 mm²/s, extinction diameter
  0.27 vs 0.80 mm; 90 % intervals covered 89.9 % of unseen tests.
- **Ablations.** Fuel as six labels instead of two numbers: AUC 0.766; adding 139 inverse flames: 0.532; balanced
  class weights keep the ranking but worsen the Brier score (gas 0.168, droplets 0.232); removing the six flagged FLEX
  rows changes nothing material (0.830 vs 0.838).
- **Case study, Moon-base air.** A 30 % ethane jet at 34 % O₂, 8.2 psi and 1 mg/s is *estimated*: 38 % chance it
  stays lit (range 25–52 %). The same request at lunar gravity is *untested*. Pure propane at 8.2 psi is *untested*:
  NASA tested propane only at 13.7–14.7 psi; the committee proposes a test at 33.4 % O₂, 14.7 psi and 0.74 mg/s.

## Limitations

Gas jets and droplets stand in for a gas leak and a liquid spill; burning solids, the main cabin hazard, have no model
because their tables do not record pressure and outcome together. All outcome data is from microgravity, so partial
gravity is untested and refused. With 31 and 27 positive outcomes these are small-data models, and for gas jets the
choice among them is within noise. The flame simulator is illustrative: its fitting needs at least four verified
solid-fuel points and none is verified yet. ZARM drop-tower data confirms the direction of the oxygen effect, not its
values.

## Reproducibility checklist

- [x] Public data only: NASA PSI tables pinned by checksum (`python run.py fetch` re-downloads and checks them).
- [x] One command from a clean checkout: `python run.py start` (loads, cleans, trains, serves; no keys, no login).
- [x] Every score above: `python scripts/evaluate_methods.py` → `docs/methods/results.md`.
- [x] Model cards with each comparison: `data/artifacts/predict/*.card.json` (after `python run.py ingest predict`).
- [x] Figures: `python scripts/readme_assets.py` → `docs/assets/`.
- [x] Tests: `python run.py test` (backend, model parity, browser); lint: `python run.py lint`.
- [x] Decisions and reasons: README "Design decisions" and `docs/DECISIONS.md`; limits: `docs/LIMITS.md`.
